---
title: "Driving a preview"
---

Three systems, three mechanisms, one behaviour: press the key, the preview
appears; press it again, the preview goes away.

## macOS — QLPreviewPanel

The plugin launches a small bundled helper, `qlpreview`, which drives
`QLPreviewPanel` — the very panel the Finder shows. The subprocess handle is
retained, so pressing Space again, or Escape, closes the preview.

### Why not qlmanage

`/usr/bin/qlmanage -p` looks like the obvious answer and is not. It is a
debugging tool rather than the Finder's Quick Look, and it cannot show
everything the Finder can. On a video it dies outright:

```
NSInternalInconsistencyException
'Setting highlightedTimeRanges is not supported in your app.'
AVKitCore  -[AVPlayerItem setHighlightedTimeRanges:]
Movie      (/System/Library/QuickLook/Movie.qlgenerator)
```

Apple's own movie generator calls an AVKit method that AVKit refuses inside
`qlmanage`. Driving `QLPreviewPanel` instead renders whatever the Finder
renders, third-party Quick Look extensions included. `qlmanage` is kept only as
a fallback for the case where the helper cannot be deployed.

## Linux — GNOME Sushi over D-Bus

```sh
dbus-send --session --print-reply --reply-timeout=10000 \
  --dest=org.gnome.NautilusPreviewer \
  /org/gnome/NautilusPreviewer org.gnome.NautilusPreviewer.ShowFile \
  string:file:///path int32:0 boolean:true
```

::: {.callout-warning title="--print-reply is not there for its output"}
Leaving it off is not a small difference. Without it `dbus-send` writes the
message and exits within milliseconds. Sushi is started by D-Bus on demand and
takes about a second to come up, and `dbus-daemon` **discards a message queued
for an activation as soon as the connection that sent it goes away**. The
service then starts, is never told what to show, and quits again on its
twelve-second idle timeout.

Nothing appears and nothing is logged. The failure is completely silent, which
is what makes it worth a warning box. Waiting for the reply keeps the connection
open until the call has been delivered.
:::

The reply is also the only sign the plugin gets that the preview service
answered at all, so the exit status is checked and a refusal — Sushi not
installed, most likely — is named in the log rather than swallowed.

The call returns as soon as the window has been handed its file, rather than
staying alive for as long as the preview, so there is no process to hold and
kill. `ShowFile`'s last argument closes the preview when the same file is
already showing, which gives Space the same toggle it has on macOS. Sushi shows
one file at a time.

## Windows — QuickLook's named pipe

[QuickLook](https://github.com/QL-Win/QuickLook) listens on a named pipe,
`QuickLook.App.Pipe.<user SID>`. One UTF-8 line through it —

```
QuickLook.App.PipeMessages.Toggle|C:\path\file.pdf|
```

— shows the preview, the same line again dismisses it, and a different path
switches to that file. So Space has its toggle here too, again with no process
to hold.

The line is written straight from the plugin through **js-ctypes**: a handful of
Win32 calls, no helper binary, no subprocess, with the SID read from the process
token. Should Gecko ever drop ctypes, a PowerShell one-liner does the same
write; it reaches the shell as `-EncodedCommand`, so no execution policy and no
command-line quoting apply to it.

An earlier attempt at this integration
([QuickLook #584](https://github.com/QL-Win/QuickLook/issues/584), 2019)
foundered on exactly that SID, and its era's conclusion — that the Store build
is sandboxed away from the pipe — was repeated for years. Measured today,
neither holds: the Store package declares `runFullTrust` and answers the pipe
like the desktop build.

::: {.callout-caution title="Never probe the pipe"}
QuickLook's pipe reader takes a line per connection and dereferences whatever it
got. A client that connects and sends nothing — a `Test-Path` on the pipe path,
any is-it-there probe — **kills the listener**, silently, until QuickLook is
restarted.

The plugin therefore never probes. Every connection it makes carries one
complete line, and "QuickLook is not running" is learned from the connect
failing, which is when it is named in the log.
:::

## EPUB, everywhere

No system preview renders an EPUB, so this is the one format the plugin
transforms rather than hands over. Everything else — MOBI, DJVU, whatever a
preview extension claims — goes to the panel untouched.

The plugin unpacks the archive into a temp directory, parses
`META-INF/container.xml` and the OPF package document, and walks the spine in
reading order, appending each chapter's `<body>` into a single output document.
The book's own stylesheets, linked and inline, are pulled in so the original
layout survives, with a Palatino base font, an 80 px margin and a 720 px
book-width column applied on top. Relative URLs in markup **and in CSS** are
rewritten to absolute `file://` paths, so images, fonts and inline SVGs resolve.

Parsing and assembly go through `DOMParser` and run on the document tree, so
scripts and inline event handlers are removed as **nodes** rather than matched
as text. A converted book is cached and reused until its file changes.

Unpacking uses `/usr/bin/unzip` on macOS and Linux, and `tar.exe` — the bsdtar
Windows has shipped since Windows 10 — on Windows, which has no `unzip`.

Because the plugin cannot reliably tell whether an EPUB preview extension is
installed, the conversion is a setting rather than a guess.
